title: Viral Videos for Social Media
lede: Eleven short-video formats that stop the scroll on Reels, TikTok, Shorts and YouTube. Each one has the idea, the beats, ideas for your niche, and the exact image, motion and script prompts. Pick one and the agent makes the whole video for you.
rules: Nobody opens social media to be sold to. Make something they would watch even if it were not an ad.
The first two seconds are the whole game. Lead with the strangest picture you have.
A good-looking clone is the easy part. The idea and the hook do most of the work.
Make people laugh and they start to like you. People buy from brands they like.
Every video wears out. Plan a fresh version every few weeks.

pipeline.detail: Choose the one that fits your customer's problem. Click Make this video.
Your business, your customer, your offer. The agent writes the script and shows it to you first.
The agent makes every character and scene as an image with Nano Banana 2.1, so the look stays the same from shot to shot.
Each still becomes a short talking clip with Veo 3.1 or Kling. Voiceover comes from your ElevenLabs voice. Songs come from ElevenLabs Music.
The agent cuts the clips in FilmCraft, burns in captions, adds the call to action and exports 9:16 to your project's exports folder.

tools.name: Nano Banana 2.1 (GenMedia)
tools.detail: Characters, scenes, mascots, style changes. Keep one image per character and reuse it.

tools.name: Veo 3.1 and Kling (GenMedia)
tools.detail: Turns each still into a 5 to 8 second clip, with lip sync when a character talks.

tools.detail: Narration in your own cloned voice, or one of your saved voices.

tools.name: FilmCraft
tools.detail: The timeline. The agent cuts, captions and exports, and you can edit by hand at any time.

formats.name: Bobblehead
formats.tag: Same script. Every person on screen gets a giant head.
formats.when: You already have a script that works but looks like every other ad. This changes only the picture.
steps: Keep a script you already have. The joke is visual: each speaker gets a huge caricature head on a normal body.
Open on the silliest action you can picture: your bobblehead self on a scooter, a zip line or a runaway office chair.
Cut fast through bobblehead versions of each type of customer, one benefit per line.
Burn in a caption for every line. End on one clear call to action.
why: The odd proportion registers before a single word is heard.
It is silly in a warm way, and that makes people like you.
It fits any niche because the gag is the look, not the topic.
It is cheap to test: you reuse a script you already have.

formats.name: Things That Talk
formats.tag: Something in your business that never talks starts talking.
formats.when: Your product or service is ordinary, and you need a reason for people to watch.
steps: List the objects in your customer's world: the house, the shoebox of receipts, the leaky faucet, the unused gym bag.
Give each object a complaint that is really your customer's problem. The faucet: "Drip. Drip. Eleven days, and nobody's called."
Let two or three objects grumble to each other. Your business shows up at the end as the fix.
Add a small sight gag and a sound: the cat batting the drip, a sigh, a squeak.
why: Nobody expects a faucet to speak, so the thumb stops.
The complaint states the pain without a lecture.
A good talking object can come back in a whole series, like a mascot.
beats: Your fix and call to action

formats.name: The Problem Speaks
formats.tag: The customer's problem gets a face and a voice: a grumpy weed, a smug cavity.
formats.when: Your customer's problem is a little gross, boring or embarrassing to talk about directly.
steps: Name the problem in one word: weeds, plaque, clutter, debt, a slow laptop.
Make it a character. A villain brags about the damage ("I'm Rusty. I'm the rust in your pipes."). A sad hero tells its story.
Bring in your service as the twist: the cleaning, the spray, the tune-up that throws the villain out.
Answer one objection in the dialogue, then end on a specific offer.
why: People see their own problem with a face, and it sticks.
A villain can say gross things in a funny way.
The before and after happen inside a story, so it never feels like a pitch.

formats.name: Don't Buy This
formats.tag: Customers beg you not to buy. Every complaint is really a result.
formats.when: You have real results to talk about, and plain testimonials feel like bragging.
steps: Write fake complaints where the complaint is the benefit: "Now I have too many customers."
Use believable customer types, each with a funny problem their success caused.
Repeat the hook between lines: "Don't sign up." "Do not click." "Seriously, don't."
Stack a second gag on top (bobbleheads, a crowd with signs) and end on a mock WARNING card.
why: Telling people not to do something makes them curious.
It lists your results as proof without sounding like bragging.
The humor makes people like you, and people buy from brands they like.
beats: 4 to 6 complaints that are really results
Each one sillier than the last

formats.name: Mockumentary Double Take
formats.tag: An office mockumentary built on a line that sounds naughty and is not.
formats.when: Your audience is a little cheeky, and your message is "stop doing it the boring way".
steps: Use the workplace-mockumentary look everyone knows: awkward coworkers and interviews straight to camera.
Write one line with a double meaning: "Nobody wants to see your junk", where the junk is boring ads.
Put the reveal in the middle: "What exactly are we filming?" "His ads."
Turn the joke into the lesson, then the call to action, then one last sign gag.
why: A familiar format with surprising words keeps people watching to the reveal.
The "did they just say that?" moment drives comments and shares.
The lesson sits inside the joke.

"He showed up with a huge package"
"Your pipes are making noises again"

formats.name: The Interpreter
formats.tag: An over-the-top everyday moment, plus a calm character who explains what is really going on.
formats.when: Your customer's problem shows up as a mood or a behavior, and they blame themselves.
steps: Show the problem as an extreme everyday moment: snapping at the toaster, crying at a dog food ad.
Add an interpreter character in a lab coat and a cap that says what it translates (SLEEP, GUT, DOG BARK). It explains the real cause, very calmly.
Repeat two or three times, each worse than the last, then bring in the product as the fix.
End on a reframe: "It's not you. It's your [cause]. We can help."
why: Viewers see their own life, so they tag their friends.
The interpreter takes the blame off the customer.
A bright illustrated look stands out in a feed of live action.
beats: Reframe line and call to action

formats.name: The Obvious Actor
formats.tag: You, in a ridiculous costume, as an obviously fake happy customer.
formats.when: Real testimonials are true but boring, and you are willing to laugh at yourself.
steps: Make a character nobody could think is real: a giant fake beard, a bucket hat, a name tag.
Show the before ("I had zero leads") and the after ("I had to hire my cousin").
Keep it short. The obvious fakeness is the joke.
Make the costume version of your clone with Nano Banana. No dressing up needed.
why: Entertaining beats credible-but-boring. People actually watch this testimonial.
Laughing at yourself makes you easy to like.
The character can come back in ad after ad.

formats.name: The Jingle
formats.tag: A catchy song about your customer's problem, sung by a cartoon version of you.
formats.when: You want something people replay, hum and send to friends.
steps: Give ElevenLabs Music your business, the customer's pain, what they want, and the result. That is good copywriting set to a beat.
Make a cartoon you the lead singer, with quick before-and-after scenes of customers.
Put the key lyric words on screen as captions, and "link below" on signs in the scenes.
why: A song is the opposite of a normal ad, so people stop for it.
A catchy hook gets replayed and remembered.
The lyrics carry the pain, the want and the call to action without a pitch.

formats.name: Clone Anywhere
formats.tag: Your AI clone, dropped somewhere unexpected or redrawn in a new style.
formats.when: You post talking-head videos and they look the same every time.
steps: Pick a look: realistic clone, 3D cartoon, comic book, retro video game, paper cutout, claymation.
Put the clone somewhere better than your office: a sunflower field, a subway car, a bowling alley.
Add one odd thing in the background (a man in a hot dog costume) and never mention it.
It does not have to be perfect. A slightly rough clone can still travel.
why: Same message, a picture they have not seen.
You never film, set up lights or learn lines.
The odd background detail keeps people watching to figure it out.
beats: Clone in a surprising place or style

formats.name: Spokes-Character
formats.tag: An AI spokesperson or a brand mascot that shows up in every video.
formats.when: You need a steady face for your ads without actors, models or shoot days.
steps: Match the spokesperson to your buyer. People trust someone who looks like them.
Make two or three spokespeople and test them against each other.
Or make a mascot that becomes the brand: an animal, an object, a little creature.
Lock one character sheet per character, so the face is the same in every video.
why: No models, actors or shoot days.
The same face in every ad builds recognition.
A mascot lets a small business be as memorable as a big one.
beats: Make many short videos with the same face

An animal mascot with a signature accessory

example.prompt: Character sheet of a brand mascot for a home insurance company: a friendly round orange owl wearing a tiny blue hard hat and a reflective safety vest, Pixar-style 3D. Full body front view, three-quarter view, side view, and four facial expressions (happy, surprised, serious, laughing) in a row. Plain light-grey background, clean studio light, 16:9. No text.

formats.name: Sky Tour
formats.tag: Aerial and walk-through shots of a property, made from photos instead of a drone.
formats.when: You sell or rent a place, and a drone crew costs more than the listing budget.
steps: Start from real photos of the property, so the video shows what is really there.
Give each photo one slow camera move: pull back, fly over, push in.
Put the key facts on screen: size, location, bedrooms and baths.
Music only. Nobody needs to talk.
why: It looks like a big-budget shoot for a few dollars.
Moving shots get far more attention than still photos.
It is quick to make again for every new listing.
beats: Hero aerial with size and location
Main bedroom or bath, with the bed and bath count
Agent name and call to action

prompts.label: Motion (from a listing photo)
prompts.text: Use this listing photo as the first frame. Slow cinematic drone pull-back that reveals [the house, the pool and the hills]. Golden hour, smooth stabilized motion, no people, do not add or change any buildings or features. 8 seconds.

prompts.label: Motion (inside)
prompts.text: Use this interior photo. Slow gimbal push-in through [the living room toward the big windows], soft daylight, realistic, keep every piece of furniture and finish exactly as shown. 6 seconds.

prompts.label: On-screen text
prompts.text: [4,200 sq ft] / [Scottsdale, AZ] / [5 bed · 4 bath] / [Agent name] · [Book a showing]

prompts.label: Shot list
prompts.text: I am listing [property: size, location, features]. Give me a 30-second vertical video shot list of 6 shots, each with: which photo to use, the camera move, the on-screen text, and the length.

formats.brief:
Make a 30-second Sky Tour video of a property from its photos: slow aerial and walk-through moves, facts on screen, music only.
Property photos: [file, several]
Size: [square feet]
Location: [city]
Bedrooms and baths: [for example 5 bed, 4 bath]
Agent name and call to action: [name and call to action]

Never add or change anything about the property in the video.

example.prompt: Cinematic aerial drone photo at golden hour of a modern single-story desert home with a turquoise pool, white stucco walls, large glass windows and palm trees, saguaro cacti and rocky hills in the background, warm sunset light, wide shot from above and behind, photorealistic real estate photography, 16:9. No text, no people.
